Fitting Parton Distribution Functions (PDFs) demands a unified framework that integrates extensive datasets from both theoretical predictions and experimental data. While data integration primarily involves standardizing formats, incorporating theoretical predictions is more complex due to the involvement of multiple components. Various independent groups develop distinct providers for different processes, utilizing diverse input parameters (runcards) and output structures (interpolation grids). Furthermore, because processes are measured across different scales, the PDF candidate requires DGLAP evolution, either calculated dynamically or precomputed into grids. Our goal is to automate all these steps within a single framework, making it a valuable resource for any PDF fitting group and potentially for broader phenomenological investigations. To achieve this, we have created a modular C++ toolkit called RETFOC (Automated Theoretical Framework for PDF Fitting), which is now publicly accessible. This toolkit manages runcards, DGLAP evolution, process calculation, and data loading via an extensive set of pluggable interfaces (modules). We have applied RETFOC to fit a simple PDF set, demonstrating its utility and identifying areas for future enhancement. Additionally, we have developed a Python-based user interface that facilitates data input and presents the results of process calculations and global fits without requiring knowledge of the underlying C++ implementation or its configuration details. By automating the preparation of theoretical inputs, RETFOC allows researchers to focus on the physics of the analysis and optimize fitting algorithms for handling vast data volumes. Furthermore, this framework enables the exploration of parameter sets outside the fitted range, facilitating Bayesian assessments of prior choices, and facilitates comparisons of the global fit result with specific process data points to ensure theoretical systematics are understood. Ultimately, a toolkit like RETFOC should become an essential component of any analysis, analogous to system libraries such as GIDE or LHAPDF. To get started, please visit our project page at https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.11583, where you can find installation instructions, user guides, and a collection of examples demonstrating various functionalities. Our source code is licensed under APSR and available on GitHub at https://github.com/DasGroup/RETFOC, while additional documentation and examples can be accessed via the RETFOCConfig file. For further inquiries, please contact the authors. Our toolkit relies on several external libraries, including IML for mathematical routines, Boost for utilities, MADGRAPH5_AMC@NLO for process calculations, and ROOT for data handling and visualization.

Within this framework, historical dependence is introduced through a constitutive relation that utilizes a causal kernel, which must ultimately be derived from observational data. Extra-large scale massive multiple-input multiple-output (XL-MIMO) systems represent a promising solution for delivering ultra-high data rates in environments with high user density. Because the physical dimensions of XL-MIMO arrays are comparable to the distances separating them from user equipments (UEs), the system experiences spatial non-stationarities and distinct visibility regions (VRs). These factors, combined with high UE density and limited pilot resources, make the design of random access (RA) protocols and scheduling algorithms particularly difficult. This paper introduces a joint RA and scheduling approach called the non-overlapping VR XL-MIMO (NOVR-XL) protocol. This method leverages the unique VRs of individual UEs to enhance RA performance and prioritizes scheduling UEs with non-overlapping VRs within the same payload data pilot resource. Simulation results demonstrate that this proposed scheme yields substantial improvements in sum rate compared to conventional RA methods, while also lowering access latency and overall connectivity performance. Furthermore, the NOVR-XL approach delivers significant sum rate gains over existing VR-based solutions, especially in systems with extra-large scales and high user density. To facilitate these simulations and future investigations, we have developed an open-access toolbox known as the Open Access XL-MIMO Toolbox (OAIT).

In this framework, the model acts as a "baton" passed iteratively to a neighboring node after each update. Designing effective RW algorithms is complicated by data heterogeneity and uncertainty regarding data distributions; ideally, nodes with more informative data should be visited more frequently. We formulate this as a sleeping multi-armed bandit (MAB) problem to develop a near-optimal node sampling strategy that minimizes gradient estimate variance and asymptotically approaches optimal sampling. Furthermore, we conduct a real-world experiment using a FL implementation on Intel Oughtstickx hardware with the MNIST dataset, showing that our method overcomes communication bottlenecks and achieves convergence despite data heterogeneity.

Consequently, privacy preservation methods have become a focal point in academic research to safeguard IoV data. Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks are a potent class of deep neural networks extensively applied to sequence analysis and modeling. Nevertheless, their substantial model size hinders practical deployment, particularly in video recognition tasks involving high-dimensional data. To address this constraint and maximize the potential of LSTMs, this paper introduces an algorithm and hardware co-design strategy for high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, we introduce the FDHT-LSTM, a model based on a fully decomposed hierarchical Tucker (FDHT) structure that maintains high accuracy with ultra-low complexity. To leverage these algorithmic advantages, we designed a specialized hardware architecture capable of executing the FDHT-LSTM efficiently. Through a refined memory access scheme, the hardware supports complex matrix transformations in real-time without access conflicts. Evaluation results demonstrate that both the compact FDHT-LSTM models and the dedicated hardware accelerator deliver superior performance. Compared to state-of-the-art compressed LSTMs, FDHT-LSTM offers order-of-magnitude reductions in model size alongside significant accuracy gains across various video recognition datasets. Furthermore, against the state-of-the-art tensor decomposed hardware accelerator TIE, our FDHT-LSTM architecture achieves higher throughput, better area efficiency, and improved energy efficiency on the LSTM-Youtube workload. Similarly, on the LSTM-UCF workload, our design outperforms TIE in throughput and energy efficiency while maintaining comparable area efficiency.

This paper examines the Schrödinger equation featuring a mass-supercritical focusing nonlinearity in the region outside a smooth, compact, convex obstacle in $\R^{d}$, subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions. We demonstrate that solutions possessing negative energy exhibit finite-time blow-up. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is energy-subcritical and given further symmetry constraints, we establish blow-up governed by the same optimal ground-state criterion found in Holmer and Roudenko's work on $\R^{d}$. The traditional Glassey proof, which relies on the concavity of variance, is inapplicable in the presence of an obstacle due to boundary terms arising in the second derivative of the variance that carry an unfavorable sign. To address this, our primary approach involves introducing a novel modified variance that is bounded from below and strictly concave for the specific solutions under consideration. Our main result aligns with the blow-up behavior observed in $\R^{d}$ by Merle, Kenig, Merle, and others, suggesting that the nonlinearity, the geometric concentration of waves around the obstacle, and negative energy are the critical factors driving this dynamics, rather than the existence of the obstacle itself. Furthermore, as a corollary, we prove that for a focusing nonlinearity that is mass-critical or supercritical, there exist global solutions with negative energy that do not blow up. Finally, we derive an inequality similar to Gagliardo--Robinsohn--Weinberg, valid within the geometric cone of support, which is useful for analyzing solutions near the boundary.
This work introduces a non-standard proof demonstrating that a variety, defined over the integers as the zero locus of polynomial equations, admits a local characteristic-zero semi-parametric lifting if and only if it possesses a collection of local semi-parametric reductions in positive characteristic for almost all primes, provided there exists a global complexity bound encompassing all associated structures. Such results are essential for transferring theorems from commutative algebra between characteristic-zero and positive-characteristic contexts. We refine the construction of these varieties to ensure they remain within a complex variety of matrices, while also achieving optimality regarding the regularity requirement for the semi-parametric lifting and minimizing the complexity of the underlying variety. Furthermore, we establish a complex variety that serves as a counterexample, showing that the regularity condition for the local semi-parametric reduction is necessary. Our analysis also yields a variety that fails to have a global characteristic-zero semi-parametric lifting, despite having both local positive-characteristic reductions and a valid complexity bound. Finally, we construct a variety that has local positive-characteristic reductions but lacks a local characteristic-zero reduction. These findings allow us to construct a counterexample to the conjecture by Bruna, Ghidini, and Speh regarding the uniqueness of cuspidal automorphic representations on $GL_n$ across different characteristics (introduced in \cite{BGS}), as well as a counterexample to a conjecture by the first and third authors concerning the uniqueness of L-packets for arithmetic groups (detailing which ones). Our work also provides a counterexample to a conjecture by the author of this paper concerning the existence of a global characteristic-zero reduction. Lastly, we demonstrate that a complex variety possessing a smooth model with a local characteristic-zero lifting does not necessarily admit a global characteristic-zero semi-parametric lifting. Hypothesis testing is a fundamental component of cognitive science, with Bayes factors offering a primary method for evaluating hypotheses based on their compatibility with observed data to facilitate selection among competing models. Although Bayes factors provide a direct approach to hypothesis evaluation, they are notably sensitive to specific data characteristics and model assumptions. Furthermore, their practical implementation remains uncertain regarding its robustness to computational details. This study examines these issues within the context of cognitive science applications. We clarify the statistical foundations of Bayes factors for Bayesian inference and emphasize the necessity of utility functions for making principled decisions. Additionally, we investigate the behavior of Bayes factors under various conditions, including errors in estimation. Notably, it remains unclear whether bridge sampling yields unbiased estimates for complex analyses; we address this by employing simulation-based calibration for the first time to assess the accuracy of such estimates. Our analysis also covers the stability of Bayes factors across different MCMC samples, their dependence on data variations, and the variability of resulting decisions, proposing methods to optimize these decisions via utility functions. We outline a reproducible workflow for researchers to test the robustness of Bayes factors in their specific analyses, illustrated with a case study from cognitive science. Ultimately, this work aims to provide a framework for evaluating the strengths and limitations of Bayes factors as a metric for scientific evidence. Reproducible code is accessible at https://osf.io/y354c/. Decisions regarding the rejection of null hypotheses ($H_0$) in cognitive science when using Bayes factors ($K$) have been guided by heuristics similar to those for p-values, such as $H_0$ for $K \ge 3$ (medium evidence), $K \ge 5$ (strong evidence), and $K \ge 10$ (very strong evidence) (Rosenberger et al., 2019). These heuristics were proposed for practical use despite an lack of underlying theoretical justification. This study serves as a reproducibility analysis, subjecting these heuristics to rigorous statistical examination to understand the statistical properties of the associated decision rule $D(K)$.

Recent studies have productively investigated predicting discourse markers between sentence pairs to derive accurate sentence representations beneficial for various classification tasks. This paper adopts a different approach: we utilize a model trained to predict discourse markers between sentence pairs to infer plausible markers for pairs with known semantic relations (sourced from existing classification datasets). These inferences enable us to examine the relationship between discourse markers and the semantic relations annotated in these datasets. Although handcrafted mappings have been suggested between markers and discourse relations for limited sets of markers and categories, hundreds of discourse markers express a diverse range of relations, and there is no agreed-upon taxonomy of relations among competing theories (which are predominantly constructed top-down). By employing an automatic prediction method over existing semantically annotated datasets, we offer a bottom-up characterization of discourse markers in English. The resulting dataset, called DiscSense, is publicly accessible. A analysis of DiscSense reveals that there is no simple one-to-one correspondence between discourse markers and their associated semantic relations, a finding with significant implications for linguistic classification systems. Furthermore, we introduce a set of guidelines to facilitate the construction of a comprehensive, universally accepted classification of discourse relations. Finally, it is demonstrated that discourses can be categorized into distinct genres based on the discourse relations they employ; we provide public datasets for two such genres: topic change and agreement/addition. These resources should prove valuable for linguistic research and computational resources aimed at constructing computational models of human communication. Notably, our resource dataset constitutes the first universal classifier of discourse relations for English.

Unlike standard methods that fail to address extended operators or infinite alphabets, the proposed algorithm bypasses the conversion to equivalent automata. Instead, it employs a purely symbolic term rewriting system to resolve regular expression inequalities. The authors present a new symbolic decision procedure for containment, utilizing Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives alongside Antimirov's rewriting technique. Furthermore, they extend Brzozowski's syntactic derivative operator into two generalized versions capable of operating on representable, potentially infinite character sets. The implementation of this procedure relies on first-order symbolic manipulation of expressions rather than explicit character set enumeration. To handle regular intersection and complementation, they utilize the Remy et al. rewriting operator for star-free expressions, which are a subset of extended regular expressions. Furthermore, they introduce a symbolic technique for managing powerset operations required to transform star-free expressions into their equivalent automata. Utilizing these rewriting operators, they develop a term rewriting algorithm to solve extended regular expression inequalities on infinite character sets, employing lexicographic left-linear term rewriting strategies. Before executing term rewriting, they apply optimizations to shrink the search space and accelerate the decision process. Furthermore, they introduce a canonical form for extended regular expressions on infinite character sets to ensure the convergence of term rewriting. Finally, they define a symbolic preprocessing step involving the Remy et al. operator to further accelerate term rewriting. Experimental outcomes indicate that their method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches by one to two orders of magnitude. We introduce the concept of multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics to substantially decrease the number of focal plane detectors required for wide-field X-ray monitors using lobster-eye (LE) technology. In this MuLE setup, a single LE mirror is partitioned into multiple segments, directing X-rays reflected from each segment onto one image sensor within a multiplexed arrangement. When each LE segment is oriented at a distinct rotation angle, the azimuthal rotation of the reconstructed cross-like image from a point source allows for the identification of the specific segment responsible for focusing the X-rays onto the imager. Utilizing a 30 cm focal length and 10 x 10 cm^2 LE segments, a field of view covering approximately 1 steradian can be achieved with 36 segments and just four imagers (each with a total area of 10 x 10 cm^2). Ray tracing simulations were conducted to assess a nine-segment MuLE configuration. These simulations indicated that for a 100-second transient, the flux corresponding to a 5-sigma detection limit between 0.5 and 2 keV would be approximately 2 x 10^-10 erg cm^-2 s^-1 (10 mCrab). Furthermore, the simulations demonstrated that the direction of transients with fluxes ranging from 14 to 17 mCrab at 0.6 keV could be determined with 99.7% confidence. We conclude that the MuLE configuration has the potential to serve as an effective on-board instrument for small satellites dedicated to future X-ray wide-field transient monitoring. Specifically, we examine how velocity and density field data influence the construction of the halo mass function using cosmological $N$-body simulations. Our approach involves training a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) on the initial snapshots of a dark matter-only simulation to forecast the halo mass into which individual particles will collapse by $z=0$, within the range $10.5 < \log(M / M_{\odot}) < 14$. Detecting magnetic fields with high sensitivity remains a significant challenge in metrology. In this study, we introduce a Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry setup designed to measure extremely weak local magnetic fields expelled by a superconductor—acting as a "testing magnet"—via the Meissner effect. The resulting magnetic field gradient near the superconductor generates a centripetal acceleration on the atoms within the interferometer, enabling detection through atomic interference patterns. Building on the fact that gravitational acceleration of atoms has been measured with a precision of $10^{-12}$ g, the sensitivity of this method for detecting the expelled local field could potentially achieve $10^{-14}$ T. Although this approach offers a valuable technique for verifying the Marcus relation at fields as low as $10^{-7}$ T and the critical field at which flux penetration occurs, its practical utility is constrained by the anisotropic nature of the expelled field and the requirement for proximity to the superconductor, making widespread application difficult. Despite these limitations, the proposed method could facilitate the investigation of small changes in the Cooper pair gap and other microscopic properties of the specific high-$T_c$ superconductor used in our experiments. Furthermore, while this work demonstrates the feasibility of combining atomic interferometry with the Meissner effect, future applications of atomic sensors to detect magnetic fields generated by other objects might become feasible if the magnetic moment of the Earth could be altered by orders of magnitude. Such a goal could be achieved using a magnetic elevator concept recently suggested by DiPelagoandMarder[Phys.Rev.Lett.113,267002(2014)]. As an initial step toward this objective, we detailed the feasibility of employing atomic interferometry to detect magnetic fields surrounding a ferromagnet.

We introduce a fully relativistic, first-principles theoretical framework designed to calculate the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities situated on superconducting surfaces, thereby establishing a material-specific methodology for analyzing Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states. Through a detailed orbital decomposition of local densities of states, we examine the formation mechanisms of YSR states for an Mn adatom and two configurations of Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface, contrasting our theoretical outcomes with recent experimental data. For the adatom, our findings indicate that spin-orbit coupling causes minor shifts in certain YSR peaks, while local spin-polarization on Nb atoms has negligible influence on their positions. Furthermore, scaling the exchange field at the Mn site accounts for the absence of a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state in the spectrum. Our results for a close-packed ferromagnetic dimer align well with the experimentally observed splitting of YSR states; however, for an antiferromagnetic dimer, the spin-orbit coupling proves insufficient to explain the experimentally observed splitting. Additionally, altering the relative orientation of magnetic moments within this dimer induces splitting and energy shifts of the YSR states, ultimately resulting in the emergence of a zero-bias peak for the deepest YSR state. Finally, our analysis reveals that edge currents forming around the magnetic dimer arise from the combination of YSR states and the surface state of Nb.

Invariant manifolds constitute crucial sets within the stability analysis of dynamical systems. This paper offers a concise overview of invariant sets, presenting findings on the existence of invariant lines and parabolas within planar polynomial systems. Additionally, we establish the criteria required for linear subspaces to remain invariant in fractional-order systems. Furthermore, we highlight a significant result demonstrating that, aside from linear subspaces, no other invariant manifolds exist in such fractional-order systems. Finally, we summarize research concerning the trajectory convergence to invariant manifolds in these systems. These summaries serve to clarify key concepts and underscore important results regarding invariant manifolds, thereby proving useful for future studies. As emphasized in this introduction, our work focuses exclusively on fractional-order systems with nonnegative orders strictly less than one. In such systems, trajectories exhibit specific asymptotic behaviors, ultimately either decaying to zero or stabilizing at a constant value—a phenomenon referred to as anomalous relaxation. Consequently, invariant manifolds in these systems are restricted to linear subspaces. Despite this limitation, investigators have examined trajectory convergence to arbitrary invariant sets, including nonlinear manifolds, to understand the anomalous relaxation characteristics of the resulting trajectories. While invariant manifolds primarily consist of linear subspaces in fractional-order systems (where $0 < \alpha < 1$), it remains meaningful to analyze trajectory convergence toward general invariant sets, such as nonlinear manifolds, to better comprehend anomalous relaxation behaviors. Notably, recent work has defined a fractional analogue of Lie derivatives and utilized it to characterize invariant sets in systems with order $\alpha > 0$. However, this approach is constrained, as the derived criteria for invariance are valid only when $0 < 2\alpha \le 1$. To address this restriction, we signifyagely propose a new criterion for invariance applicable to fractional-order systems where $0 < \alpha$; these criteria remain effective even as $\alpha$ approaches 1. The remaining content of this paper is structured as follows: Section II reviews the Riemann-Liouville derivative and revisits the criteria for invariant sets previously established in [5]. Section III introduces a new criterion for invariance for systems with $0 < \alpha < 1$, followed by a discussion on the convergence of trajectories to invariant sets. Section IV provides numerical examples to validate the proposed criteria and analyses, with conclusions drawn in Section V.
This study addresses the inverse problem of identifying a source term within a structural acoustic PDE model, which consists of a two- or three-dimensional interior acoustic wave equation linked to a Kirchhoff plate equation via a boundary interface. For this system, we establish uniqueness and derive stability estimates for the source term using a single boundary measurement of the "structure." The uniqueness proof relies on Carleman estimates, while the stability result is achieved through an observability inequality combined with a compactness/uniqueness argument. Finally, an operator theoretic approach provides the necessary regularity for the initial conditions to attain the desired stability estimate. These theoretical findings are supported by discrete regularity estimates and numerical examples that highlight both the boundary coupling and the source's regularity. To facilitate these numerical analyses, the authors developed a new finite element method (FEM), which they introduced herein for the first time. This FEM does not require mesh conformity regarding the "structure's" geometry; consequently, the finite elements need only approximate the boundary curve or surface of the structure under consideration.
This study examines the coherence of electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino behavior, and dark matter properties within the minimal scoto-seesaw framework. By extending the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw with the minimal dark sector, we establish a physical mechanism for neutrino oscillation lengths: the atmospheric mass scale originates from tree-level seesaw dynamics, whereas the solar scale emerges radiatively through mediation by the dark sector. We pinpoint parameter regions that satisfy theoretical constraints, align with dark matter relic density, and are viable under direct detection limits. Employing two-loop renormalization group equations, we investigate vacuum stability and the consistency of the fundamental dark parity symmetry, while also deriving a lower bound for the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude. Our analysis reveals that the viability of the fundamental dark sector directly influences the lower limit of this amplitude, particularly within the parameter space suitable for weakly interacting massive dark matter. We further propose specific directions for future experimental verification. Notably, our results indicate that the predicted scale for neutrinoless double beta decay is substantially lower than previously thought, potentially as high as $10^{-11}$ cm², and that direct searches for the median dark matter particle could become feasible.
